Commentary.Commentary: Welcome back for Zimbabwe's response with the bat. The Pakistani players scatter out of the huddle and take their spots on the field. Tadiwanashe Marumani and Brian Bennett walk out to open for the Chevrons. Naseem Shah has the new ball and is raring to go. A slip in place. Brian to face. Here we go...
... THE RUN CHASE ...

Okay then, Zimbabwe have a huge mountainous task to complete. They will have to bat out of their skins to achieve this target. Is it tough? Absolutely not. But challenging, sure. 194 is the highest successful run chase at Rawalpindi, so it's almost in that territory. And for scaling it, Zimbabwe will have to produce a strong opening partnership. Also, their fragile middle order will need to step up and reduce the load from Sikandar Raza's shoulders. Pakistan will be eyeing three wins in as many matches and confirm their finale spot. Back in a bit with the chase very shortly.

Pakistan's Babar Azam is up for a quick chat. He says that today it felt like the Pindi pitch they generally know and the ball was coming onto the bat nicely. Adds that he and Farahn focused on not just hitting boundaries but building a big stand as well. Reckons that after the first 6 overs, you get a clearer picture of what kind of a total is suitable on the track, as early on there is a bit of help for the seamers as well. Also adds that the weather does also play a part in the surface playing differently but believes that as a batter, you need to be prepared to play in any conditions.

Despite a quiet phase, Zimbabwe couldn't break this partnership. Their spinners were a bit too flat and quick on occasion. Pakistan's greatest asset during this phase was the manner in which Babar and Farhan consistently rotated the strike, accumulating singles and doubles even when boundaries dried up. The partnership flourished to 103 before Raza finally dismissed Sahibzada. Babar subsequently rediscovered his touch and began dispatching deliveries with authority. His excellent knock of 72 eventually ended during the closing stages. Pakistan slipped a bit towards the backend, from 144/2 to 167/5, but Fakhar Zaman came out all guns blazing and with his breezy cameo of 27 off just 10 balls, Pakistan managed to post 195 on the board.

Confidence is a tonic, and Farhan had it all. He was effortless in finding the gaps even after the restrictions were lifted. After having the worst Powerplay with the ball in this series, Zimbabwe tried a few tricks and took the pace off to deceive the batters on a slowish kind of a track, but remained elusive from wickets. Babar wasn't at his fluent best, and it showed as he struggled to time the ball well initially. But with wickets in hand, and the run rate still above 8 an over, it was all set up for a strong finish in the second half.

There was just a bit of microscopic movement early doors, but nothing extravagant to trouble the batters. Farhan got off the blocks instantly and so did Saim Ayub, but after a couple of consecutive sixes, Ayub's inning was cut short by Evans. Farhan, in particular, kept the aggressive intent and led the act with some scintillating hits. Babar took his time to settle in, in his usual fashion. But Pakistan ended their Powerplay on a high with 53/1 on the board.

A very, very strong finish for Pakistan. 69 runs in the last five overs, with 25 coming off the final over alone. This was one of those kinds of days when you just don't want to be a bowler. Every Pakistani batter who came to the crease, took apart the Zimbabwean bowling unit one by one. An absolute carnage is what it was, and this is the highest first inning total in this Tri-Series. The average score while batting first is around 150 mark, so Pakistan have finished well above that figure. A rather disappointing bowling display from Zimbabwe, who were so good in their first two matches.

Zaman effortlessly whips it over deep square leg for a biggie, the third one in the over and Pakistan end with a mammoth total of 195/5 on the board.

Babar Azam hasn't looked at his fluent best so far, but Sahibzada Farhan's confident presence at the other end has ensured they don't get into a cave. Pakistan will feel they are at a comfortable position with the way they are going. Zimbabwe need wickets as quickly as possible. Commentary.Commentary: All in readiness for the game to begin. The two umpires are the first ones to make their way out to the middle, followed by the players of Zimbabwe. It will be the duo of Saim Ayub and Sahibzada Farhan to open the innings for Pakistan. Richard Ngarava has the new ball in hand and he is raring to go. Let's play...

Tadiwanashe Marumani is down for a quick chat. Marumani says that he just tries to keep it simple and react to what's happening out there. Adds that his mentality is to just go out and score for the team. Mentions that as an opener with Bennett, the blueprint is to score at least 50-60 runs in the Powerplay, and also keep in mind how the pitch is playing. Admits that he expected the wicket to be a bit easier to bat on, but admits that conditions have been a bit tricky.

PITCH REPORT - Former Sri Lankan all-rounder, Russel Arnold, is pitchside. He says that the wicket is looking tired and dry and reckons that the spinners will come into play more. Feels that the pacers need to hit the deck rather than bowl full and adds that the best time to bat is with the new ball and ends by saying that Pakistan will be eyeing a total of around 155-160.

Zimbabwe (Playing XI) - Brian Bennett, Tadiwanashe Marumani, Brendan Taylor (WK), Sikandar Raza (C), Ryan Burl, Tony Munyonga, Tashinga Musekiwa, Brad Evans, Tinotenda Maposa, Richard Ngarava, and Wellington Masakadza (In for Graeme Cremer).

Pakistan (Playing XI) - Saim Ayub, Sahibzada Farhan, Babar Azam, Salman Agha (C), Usman Khan (WK), Fakhar Zaman, Mohammad Nawaz, Faheem Ashraf, Mohammad Wasim, Naseem Shah (In for Salman Mirza), and Usman Tariq (In for Abrar Ahmed).

The captain of Zimbabwe, Sikandar Raza, says that they came into this Tri-series to derail every team. Highlights that the first game against Pakistan was pretty good, and the result followed against Sri Lanka. Adds that they wanted to bowl first and challenge themselves. Informs that they have one rotational change as they wanted to give everyone a go. Ends by saying Wellington Masakadza replaces Graeme Cremer.

The captain of Pakistan, Salman Agha, says that they will bat first as it still looks like a good wicket to bat on, and they have chased in the last two games, and hence would like to bat first. Adds that Zimbabwe have been playing some good cricket, but they just want to focus on themselves. Mentions that the game against Sri Lanka was near perfect, and they would like to continue in the same way. On playing on his birthday, Salman says that he simply wants to do well in the match and nothing else.
TOSS - The flip of the coin lands in favor of Pakistan and the birthday boy, Salman Agha, elects to BAT first.

Rawalpindi is usually an express highway for batting, the kind of surface where bowlers show up knowing they are in for a long day. But this time around? The average first innings score is stuck below 150, which tells you the pitch has some bite. Bowlers are getting something out of it, especially when defending under lights. Both Pakistan and Zimbabwe have bowling attacks that are breathing fire right now, so you have to wonder how the batters are going to handle the pressure. A win will seal the finale spot for Pakistan, whereas if Zimbabwe come up trumps this time around, it will force all teams to go another mile to confirm their respective berth. It's shaping up to be an exciting game. Toss and teams coming up next very shortly. Stay tuned.

Zimbabwe pushed Pakistan to the brink in their opener, then went full savage mode and actually took down Sri Lanka in their last outing. Here's where they have been different from Pakistan. Their Powerplay bowling is locked in tight, keeping it under a run-a-ball in both games. That's genuinely impressive when you're up against higher-ranked teams with way more resources and talent depth. Brad Evans and Richard Ngarava have been relentless with the ball and need to keep that momentum rolling. Brian Bennett's bat has been hot, but the middle order? Still all over the place. Most of the pressure keeps falling on skipper Sikandar Raza to bail them out, and that's a dangerous game to keep playing.

It’s a quick turnaround for Pakistan after they decimated Sri Lanka the other day. Their batting lineup has been a trainwreck, with only Salman Agha and Sahibzada Farhan showing up when it matters. The rest? Ghost mode. The largely talked criticism for them has been not being able to keep up with the pace of modern-day T20I format, and also not playing a perfect game of cricket. Their bowling attack is absolutely carrying this team. Two games, two chases, and both times they've suffocated opponents under 150, with Mohammad Nawaz being an absolute menace with the ball. If only they could tighten up a bit in the Powerplay with the ball, they could be dangerous.

The world is wrapped up in red-ball cricket, but Rawalpindi is marching to its own beat with this T20I Tri-Series grinding forward. Match number 4 is upon us and it carries serious weight. Pakistan take on Zimbabwe again in a reverse fixture, except this time there is way more riding on it. Win here and you control your destiny. Lose and you are sweating bullets heading into the final round. The margins are razor thin. Welcome to the coverage. It’s always a pleasure.
... MATCH DAY ...

The tri-series in Rawalpindi marches on with the fourth match featuring hosts Pakistan and Zimbabwe. It is the reverse fixture between these sides who are coming off respective victories in their previous games. In the series opener, Pakistan demonstrated their strength with a commanding victory over the visitors. However, the dynamics of this contest have significantly shifted. Zimbabwe enters this match riding a huge wave of confidence, having completely dismantled Sri Lanka in their previous outing. This performance has underscored their capability to spring major surprises and compete fiercely against teams with greater exposure and experience. The Chevrons will be eager to translate this positive momentum into a tangible result, aiming to level the ledger against their hosts. This will mark the 23rd T20I meeting between the two sides. While Pakistan currently holds a slight edge in recent history, leading 3-2 in the last five encounters, the current form of both teams suggests a much tighter, hard-fought contest is on the cards. Even in their opening fixture, the Zimbabwean bowlers led by Richard Ngarava controlled the Powerplay overs. So far, they have picked up 5 wickets inside the fielding restrictions in both matches played, and have conceded just 56 runs. Brad Evans has brilliantly stepped up as in Zimbabwe’s front like of attack whereas Maposa and Cremer have been the bright spots. Batting-wise, their opening combo of Brian Bennett and Tadiwanashe Marumani have played a consistent hand, fortifying the top order, but still, the middle order relies heavily on the shoulders of skipper Sikandar Raza. This is the key area where their focus of improvement must be upon before taking the field for this game. Pakistan, meanwhile, isn’t just playing for wins anymore. They’re making statements. At home, they expect dominance, not just professionalism. Sahibzada Farhan has been absolutely scorching since the Asia Cup, leading Pakistan with 676 runs this calendar year and coming off his highest ever T20I score. Fakhar Zaman has settled into that middle order anchor role perfectly. But the elephant in the room? Babar Azam. Back in the shortest format after time away, and the returns have been painfully ordinary. Mohammad Nawaz has carried the all-rounder burden brilliantly, especially with the ball recently, but Pakistan will be aiming fire collectively if they want to completely snuff out this Zimbabwean challenge.
